summary.text: Catalina Cruz is the Democratic and Working Families Party incumbent for NY State Assembly District 39, which she has represented since 2019. An attorney who grew up undocumented in Queens, she worked in city and state government before winning the seat in 2018, and serves on the Codes, Ethics and Guidance, Health, Insurance, Labor, Rules, and Ways and Means committees. Her official biography highlights immigration reform, tenant protections and workers' rights.

paragraphs.text: Cruz was born in Colombia and came to Queens at age 9; she lived in the United States for more than 10 years as an undocumented immigrant (a "DREAMer") before gaining status.

According to her official biography, she was raised by a single mother who worked multiple jobs, including as a nanny, cleaning offices at night and selling tamales and empanadas at weekend soccer fields.

She holds a bachelor's degree from John Jay College of Criminal Justice and a Juris Doctor from the City University of New York School of Law, and is admitted to practice law in New York; Wikipedia dates the degrees to 2005 and 2009.

Before holding elected office, Cruz practiced housing law representing tenants in housing court. Her government posts included Chief of Staff to then-Council Member Julissa Ferreras-Copeland, Counsel to the City Council's Committee on Immigration, and Director of the Governor's Exploited Workers Task Force.

She won the September 13, 2018 Democratic primary for Assembly District 39 over incumbent Ari Espinal and Yonel Letellier Sosa, then won the November 6, 2018 general election; Ballotpedia lists her tenure as beginning in 2019. She has been re-elected in 2020, 2022 and 2024.

Cruz serves on the Assembly's Codes, Ethics and Guidance, Health, Insurance, Labor, Rules, and Ways and Means committees, and is a member of the Black, Puerto Rican, Hispanic & Asian Legislative Caucus, the Legislative Women's Caucus and the Task Force on New Americans.

Her official biography says she has passed more than 20 new laws since taking office in 2019, including on food insecurity, healthcare costs and protections for older New Yorkers, and that she helped secure state funding for schools, hospitals and libraries in her district.
Her district includes Corona, Elmhurst and Jackson Heights and parts of Middle Village and Rego Park, and her official biography says she lives in Jackson Heights.
